extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, IP practitioners and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for determining whether information constitutes prior art for novelty and inventive step, with special focus on internet / new media disclosures, evidentiary requirements, confidentiality, place/time effects, and treatment of pending applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and understandability to the person skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is prior art only if it was accessible and understandable to the average person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the relevant public is aware of the information and knows how to decipher it it may be considered prior art; encrypted or otherwise inaccessible information will generally not be considered prior art unless the public can access and understand it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of disclosure is irrelevant if publicly accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: The geographic place where disclosure occurred is irrelevant so long as the information is accessible by the person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure is considered prior art whether it took place domestically or abroad; the applicable law for assessing whether a disclosure occurred is the law of the country assessing novelty and inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and duration of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: There is generally no temporal limit beyond the filing date for considering a disclosure as prior art, but duration and timing can matter for internet disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jurisdictions (e.g. Japan) judge very short-lived internet postings as not publicly accessible — duration should be evaluated by time and other factors like accessibility. Archives are desirable but not always required; loss of evidence over time is analogous to fading physical copies and does not automatically require special internet rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for asserted prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof that a specific piece of information was disclosed is on the party arguing lack of novelty (e.g. examiner or challenger).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In prosecution the examiner typically must satisfy evidentiary criteria (e.g. printouts, inspection of manipulation risk). If the applicant challenges reliability, the examiner must investigate and may withdraw the citation if convincing evidence of manipulation or unreliability exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognized means/forms of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure may occur by written or oral description, use, sale, any other means, or through electronic/telecommunication means (internet, CD-ROM, TV, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No specific limitation to means: oral statements, use, printed documents, electronic records, and internet postings are all recognized; interactive internet content (e.g. websites) and one-way transmissions (TV) can constitute disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'publication' or 'published document'
rubrics_metrics.description: A publication is an information-transmitting medium copied or reproduced for distribution and disclosure to the public; electronic media (CD-ROM, etc.) are included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents prepared for publication but not dispatched (e.g. still in publisher's warehouse) may not yet be 'published'; secrecy documents or internal minutes with no distribution purpose are not publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes 'the public' (recipient criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure is prejudicial if it is made available to an undetermined number of persons or to a limited group if there is potential for propagation to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure to a limited number of persons absent confidentiality restrictions — where recipients can understand or transfer the disclosure to others — is considered public. Exhibitions and sales where the invention can be understood by inspection or disassembly are opposable as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality negates prior art (but ends if confidentiality removed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures made under confidentiality do not count as prejudicial prior art; implied confidentiality (social/business expectation) also protects disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a person bound by confidentiality later is released, or the confidentiality is not present/was not intended, the disclosure may become public. Guidelines (e.g. EPC examiner guidelines) are applied to determine confidentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of errors in disclosed information
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors in a disclosure are relevant only if they affect the content of the information that would prejudice novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the correct content is self-evident, courts may correct obvious errors; but incorrect descriptions that cannot be easily corrected should not be used as evidence to defeat novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty vs inventive step — scope of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is destroyed if a claimed invention is identical to the prior disclosure; inventive step is lacking if the claimed invention could have been made easily by a person skilled in the art based on prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art for novelty is usually confined to the same technical field, whereas prior art for inventive step may come from different fields; recombination of known elements normally affects inventive step but not necessarily novelty; strict equivalents in prior art may destroy novelty while broad equivalents generally do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pending (earlier-filed) unpublished applications
rubrics_metrics.description: An earlier-filed patent application that is pending but will be published can affect the novelty of later applications (subject to first-to-file/co-pending applicant rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier filed applications laid open later can be opposed for novelty but generally do not serve as a basis for inventive step; if inventor/applicant are same in both applications, conflicts are resolved by first-to-file/double patenting principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet/new media disclosure specifics — public accessibility tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Information on the internet constitutes a disclosure if it is accessible to the public (e.g. URL obtainable, indexed by search engines, linked from public sites, or available via mailing lists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encrypted information is not publicly accessible unless tools/keys are obtainable by unspecified persons. Password protection negates public accessibility unless the password is obtainable by the public. Paywalls do not, by themselves, prevent public accessibility judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet/new media evidentiary and authenticity measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Because internet content can be deleted or manipulated, special evidentiary steps are required to cite internet disclosures reliably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JPO guidelines: presume originality for official/quasi-official websites; examiner may contact site owner to confirm; examiner should print the page, record access date/time, URL and examiner identity, and store the printout in the office database. If manipulation risk remains, information should not be cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration and accessibility considerations for online disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Short-lived internet postings may not constitute publicly accessible information; duration must be judged by time and accessibility factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archive presence is desirable but not strictly required for novelty evaluation; examiners often print and preserve pages when citing them because of low permanency online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences among network forms (email, mailing lists, forums)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all electronic communications are equally public: private email is typically not public, while mailing lists or publicly accessible forums are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether an electronic communication is 'publicly accessible' depends on distribution to unspecified persons and the manner of transmission; interactivity and access controls affect the assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source reliability and presumption of originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Information from official or quasi-official organization websites is presumed original and not easily manipulated; other sources require assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should study likelihood of manipulation (content and upload date). If reliability is doubtful, the examiner should investigate and may withdraw the citation; contacting the responsible party is an option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to obtain invention via reverse engineering/disassembly
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention's content can be recognized by disassembly or reverse engineering using simple and well-known steps, that suffices as disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case-by-case: if additional steps are simple and known to a skilled person, novelty is lost; if the embodiment is destroyed or cannot be understood by disassembly, novelty may be retained.

rubrics_metrics.name: No special substantive rules needed for new media (general rules apply)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Italian Group's view: existing general rules for disclosure should apply to internet/new media rather than creating special substantive rules, though procedural/evidentiary measures may be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems of permanence and manipulation should be addressed by evidentiary practices rather than different substantive novelty rules.
